entities.name: Connectionism and neural networks
entities.criterion: A passage names, with one of the listed names, networks of interconnected neuron-like units (natural or artificial) as a model of computation, memory or learning; "nervous nets" and "nets of neurons" in a purely physiological description are recorded as descriptions, not as naming.

search.venues: Retrieved primary texts 1943-1997 listed under the documents of this group, the Dartmouth proposal facsimile (dataset) and Minsky 1961 (dataset transcription).
search.methods: Full-text search of each retrieved text layer for "neural net", "neuron net", "nerve net", "nervous net", "connectionis", "parallel distributed"; page images read for the scanned Dartmouth proposal, Rosenblatt 1957, Widrow and Hoff 1960, Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams 1986 and LeCun et al. 1989, which have no text layer (only the pages named in the locators were read). Citation following from Minsky 1961 and Rosenblatt 1958.
search.gaps: Minsky's 1954 Princeton dissertation, cited in Minsky 1961 as "Neural Nets and the Brain Model Problem", was not retrieved; if its title page carries that wording it would be an earlier located naming (1954). Texts of the 1940s-1950s cybernetics literature (Rashevsky, Farley and Clark, Uttley, Hebb 1949) and the Thorndike-era psychological sense of "connectionism" were not searched. Feldman and Ballard, "Connectionist models and their properties" (Cognitive Science, 1982) refused (HTTP 403). The PDP volumes were read only for chapter 8. Scanned texts were read page by page, not searched in full.
search.failures: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Feldman and Ballard 1982, HTTP 403); pnas.org and Europe PMC (Hopfield 1982, HTTP 403 and 500; the Caltech copy was used); bioinf.jku.at (LSTM, expired certificate; a course copy was used); iro.umontreal.ca (Anubis bot challenge); apps.dtic.mil (ICS Report 8506, site under maintenance).

corrections.reason: Same-family audit: Titles before 1955 found by a Crossref search name nets of neurons as formal models: W. Pitts, “The linear theory of neuron networks: The static problem” (Bull. Math. Biophys., 1942); H. D. Landahl, “A note on neural nets” (1944); Landahl and Runge, “Outline of a matrix calculus for neural nets” (1946); D. Studley, “Algebra of neural nets” (1949); A. Rapoport, “Contribution to the probabilistic theory of neural nets” (1950). None was read, so whether each meets the criterion (a model of computation, memory or learning, not a physiological description) is open.

entities.note: Rosenblatt 1958 uses "connectionist" for a theoretical position on memory and recognition and places the perceptron under it; that record is a use of the name for the family's approach. The earliest-located naming is a section heading of a research proposal and names a research problem, not a built system.

entities.criterion: The string "deep learning" (or "Deep Learning") used for learning in neural networks or comparable multi-layer architectures with several layers of learned representation; uses for depth of search, for conflict-set learning in constraint satisfaction, or for students' approaches to study are other senses.

search.venues: Retrieved primary texts of the neural-network line 1943-2015 (McCulloch and Pitts; Rosenblatt 1957 and 1958; Widrow and Hoff; Minsky 1961; Fukushima; Hopfield; Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams 1986 and the PDP chapter; LeCun et al. 1989; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber; Hinton, Osindero and Teh; Bengio et al. NIPS 2006; Bengio and LeCun 2007; Hinton 2007 (Trends in Cognitive Sciences); Ranzato et al. CVPR 2007; Weston, Ratle and Collobert ICML 2008; Bengio 2009; Goodfellow et al. 2014; LeCun, Bengio and Hinton 2015), Dechter (AAAI-86), and Schmidhuber's surveys of 2014 and 2022 for leads.
search.years: 1943-2015 for the texts read; index queries limited to 1980-2005.
search.methods: Full-text search of each retrieved text for "deep learning", "learn deep", "deep network" and "deep belief"; Semantic Scholar bulk search for "deep learning" with "neural", "network", "neurons" and for "learn deep", years 1980-2005 (2026-10-29); a Crossref bibliographic query for "deep learning" neural to 2005; citation following from Schmidhuber 2014 and 2022.
search.gaps: Aizenberg, Aizenberg and Vandewalle (2000), which Schmidhuber 2022 names as the text that brought the term to neural networks, was not retrieved (book). Gomez and Schmidhuber (GECCO 2005, "learn deep memories") was not retrieved (404). Bengio's 2007 technical report version of Learning Deep Architectures for AI (Montréal TR 1312) sits behind a bot challenge. The NIPS 2007 workshop pages were not searched. Semantic Scholar and Crossref results before 2006 are dominated by the education-research sense ("deep learning" as opposed to surface learning) and by misdated records; one unverified Semantic Scholar record dated 1999 ("DEEP LEARNING Automatic Target Recognition Using Neural Networks") could not be checked (rate limit, no full text) and is not counted. Texts read with no use of the term: Hinton, Osindero and Teh 2006; Bengio et al. 2006; Bengio and LeCun 2007; Hinton 2007; Ranzato et al. 2007; Krizhevsky et al. 2012; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997.
search.failures: Springer book page for Aizenberg et al. 2000 (bot challenge); Google Books API (HTTP 429, quota); people.idsia.ch/~juergen/gecco05gomez.pdf (HTTP 404); iro.umontreal.ca (Anubis bot challenge); now Publishers page (HTTP 403); ICML 2007 paper URL redirected to an unrelated page; Semantic Scholar single-paper search (HTTP 429).

entities.note: Schmidhuber's accounts differ between versions: the 2014 overview (v4) says the expression was coined around 2006; the 2022 history names Dechter (1986) for machine learning and Aizenberg et al. (2000) for neural networks. Both are recorded as his statements; neither is resolved.

claims.subject: dartmouth-proposal-1955
claims.statement: The Dartmouth proposal of 1955 lists "Neuron Nets" as a heading among its research problems, asking how a set of hypothetical neurons can be arranged to form concepts.

time.note: Date of the dated typescript, as already recorded in the dataset.

claims.qualification: Held the earliest-located role in the draft; the role is withheld on 2026-10-29 (see the concept's note). Found by the recorded search, not evidence of coinage; the passage names a research problem and lists earlier workers on it (Uttley, Rashevsky, Farley and Clark, Pitts and McCulloch, Minsky, Rochester, Holland), so the name was not new to the field. Minsky's 1954 dissertation title (cited as "Neural Nets and the Brain Model Problem") was not retrieved.

evidence.locator: facsimile PDF p. 3, printed p. 2, section 3
evidence.passage: Section 3 is headed "Neuron Nets" and asks how a set of (hypothetical) neurons can be arranged so as to form concepts, noting theoretical and experimental work by Uttley, Rashevsky and his group, Farley and Clark, Pitts and McCulloch, Minsky, Rochester and Holland, and that the problem needs more theoretical work.
evidence.note: Scanned PDF without a text layer: paraphrase of the page image.

claims.subject: th-rosenblatt-1958
claims.statement: Rosenblatt's 1958 Psychological Review paper says its theory takes the empiricist, or "connectionist", position and was developed for a hypothetical nervous system or machine called a perceptron.
claims.qualification: The text's "connectionist" names a theoretical position on how information is stored and recognised; the record does not show that the later family name derives from this use.

evidence.passage: The theory to be presented here takes the empiricist, or "connectionist" … The theory has been developed for a hypothetical nervous system, or machine, called a perceptron.
evidence.note: The omitted words are "position with regard to these questions", broken by the page number 387 in the text layer.

claims.subject: th-rosenblatt-1958
claims.statement: Rosenblatt (1958) uses "neural network" for a network with many random connections whose reliable functioning Ashby and von Neumann had studied.
claims.qualification: A use attributed to the problem studied by other theorists; it does not show that Rosenblatt used the term for the perceptron itself in this passage.

evidence.passage: have been concerned with the problems of how an imperfect neural network, containing many random connections, can be made to perform reliably those functions which might be represented by idealized wiring diagrams.

claims.subject: minsky-1961-steps
claims.statement: Minsky's "Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence" (1961) refers to "theories of self-organizing neural nets" and sets them aside as having motivation and methods different from heuristic programming.

time.note: Date as recorded in the dataset source (Proceedings of the IRE, January 1961).

claims.qualification: The passage names the approach to set it aside; it is not a definition. The transcription is a later HTML copy.

evidence.locator: section on models based on brain analogies (HTML transcription)
evidence.passage: Limitations of space preclude detailed discussion here of theories of self-organizing neural nets, and other models based on brain analogies.

claims.subject: th-fukushima-1980
claims.statement: Fukushima's Neocognitron paper (1980) describes its aim as synthesising a neural network model with a human-like ability of pattern recognition.
claims.qualification: A use of the name in the paper's title and introduction.

evidence.passage: In this paper, we discuss how to synthesize a neural network model in order to endow it an ability of pattern recognition like a human being.

claims.subject: th-hopfield-1982
claims.statement: Hopfield's 1982 PNAS paper is titled "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities".
claims.qualification: A title use.

evidence.passage: Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities

claims.subject: th-mcculloch-pitts-1943
claims.statement: McCulloch and Pitts state that, because of the all-or-none character of nervous activity, neural events and their relations can be treated by means of propositional logic.
claims.qualification: The paper describes nets of neurons in physiological terms ("nervous nets"); it does not use the family names searched for. Not evidence that later network models derive from it.

evidence.passage: Because of the "all-or-none" character of nervous activity, neural events and the relations among them can be treated by means of propositional logic. It is found that the behavior of every net can be described in these terms
evidence.note: Read in the 1990 reprint, which gives itself as reprinted from the 1943 volume.

claims.subject: th-rosenblatt-1957

object.value: The perceptron concept, from the author’s brain-analogue research, developed under the laboratory’s internal research program

claims.statement: The preface of Rosenblatt’s report 85-460-1 (January 1957) says that the work was supported by the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory’s internal research program, that its concepts came from the author’s research in physiological psychology aimed at a brain analogue, that the perceptron concept is “a recent product of this research program”, and that the current effort aims at the perceptron’s technical and economic feasibility.
claims.qualification: The report's own statement of its programme; it does not show that a machine had been built by that date. “This research program” in the preface is ambiguous between the laboratory’s programme and the author’s own research (audit A).

evidence.passage: The preface says the work was supported by the internal research program of the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory; that the concepts came from the author's research in physiological psychology aimed at formulating a brain analogue; that the perceptron concept is a recent product of this program; and that the current effort aims at establishing its technical and economic feasibility.
evidence.note: Scanned PDF without a text layer: paraphrase of the page image.

claims.subject: th-rosenblatt-1958
claims.statement: Rosenblatt (1958) describes the perceptron as designed to illustrate fundamental properties of intelligent systems in general without depending on the conditions of particular biological organisms.
claims.qualification: The author's description of his model; not evidence of its performance.

evidence.passage: The perceptron is designed to illustrate some of the fundamental properties of intelligent systems in general, without becoming too deeply enmeshed in the special, and frequently unknown, conditions which hold for particular biological organisms.

claims.subject: th-widrow-hoff-1960
claims.statement: Widrow and Hoff describe an adaptive "neuron" element whose input weights (gains) are set during a "training" procedure by showing it examples of inputs and desired outputs.
claims.qualification: Paraphrase of printed p. 96 only; the paper's learning rule itself was not read.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 96), sections A and B
evidence.passage: The paper describes a combinational logical circuit, the typical element of its adaptive switching circuits, which bears some resemblance to a "neuron" model of von Neumann, hence the name; the element forms a weighted sum of +1/-1 inputs with adjustable gains, outputs +1 or -1 by threshold, and its gains are set during a "training" procedure in which the designer shows the system examples of inputs and desired outputs.
evidence.note: Scanned PDF without a text layer: paraphrase of the page image.

claims.subject: th-hopfield-1982
claims.statement: Hopfield (1982) states that there are classes of physical systems whose spontaneous behaviour can serve as a general, error-correcting content-addressable memory.

openQuestions.question: Should the earliest-located naming for connectionism be the Dartmouth proposal's heading "Neuron Nets" (1955), given that the heading names a research problem and lists earlier workers?
openQuestions.recommended: Keep it, with the qualification as drafted, and give retrieval of Minsky's 1954 dissertation ("Neural Nets and the Brain Model Problem") priority in the cross-family check; if its title page is retrieved, it becomes the earliest located by correction.

openQuestions.question: The earliest located neural-sense use of "deep learning" (Weston et al., ICML 2008) is late and the abstract refers to "existing approaches to deep learning". Should the term section stay open?
openQuestions.recommended: Keep Weston 2008 as earliest located with the stated search, and ask the cross-family checker to search 2000-2008 (Aizenberg et al. 2000; NIPS 2007 workshop; Bengio TR 1312 of 2007; Gomez and Schmidhuber 2005). Any earlier text meeting the criterion becomes a correction.

openQuestions.question: Should works known only from citations (Linnainmaa 1970, Werbos 1974 and 1982, Parker 1985, LeCun 1985, Kelley 1960, Aizenberg et al. 2000) be candidate document records?
